readings.title: The Story of My Life: the word at the well-house (chapter iv)
readings.challenge: Distinguish what the young child experienced from the meaning the adult writer gives it.
readings.focus: The day Anne Sullivan arrived and the morning at the pump when Keller understood that everything has a name.
readings.context: Helen Keller (1880–1968) became deaf and blind after an illness when she was nineteen months old. She wrote The Story of My Life (1903; this is the 1905 edition) while a student at Radcliffe College. In the previous chapter her family found, through Alexander Graham Bell and the Perkins Institution for the Blind in Boston, a teacher willing to come to their home in Alabama. Laura Bridgman was a deaf and blind woman educated at Perkins decades earlier. A sounding-line measures the depth of water under a ship; in the Bible, Aaron’s rod is a staff that blossomed. The [1] after the well-house paragraph marks an editor’s note pointing to Anne Sullivan’s own letter about this day, printed later in the book.
readings.contentNote: Keller describes weeks of anger and smashing a doll in a temper. She uses “dumb” in its older sense of “unable to speak.”

excerpt.locator: Part I, Chapter IV, the whole chapter; opens “THE most important day I remember in all my life is the one on which my teacher, Anne…”; closes “…over the joys it had brought me, and for the first time longed for a new day to come.”.

questions.prompt: Keller compares herself before her teacher came to a ship in fog. What did she lack, according to the comparison?
facilitatorNotes: The ship at least has a compass and a sounding-line to find its way; she had neither, no means of knowing where she was or how near help might be. The comparison turns a state she could not describe at the time into something a sighted, hearing reader can feel. Its last sentence calls her teacher “the light of love,” which joins teaching and affection.
evidence: I was like that ship before my education began, only I was without compass or sounding-line, and had no way of knowing how near the harbour was.

questions.prompt: Keller could spell “doll,” “pin” and “hat” weeks before the well-house. Why does she say she was not really spelling words yet?
facilitatorNotes: She copied the finger movements “in monkey-like imitation” without knowing that the movements stood for things or that words existed at all. What was missing was the idea of naming. She also could not tell “mug” from “water,” because she did not yet understand that each pattern belonged to one thing.
evidence: I did not know that I was spelling a word or even that words existed; I was simply making my fingers go in monkey-like imitation.
But my teacher had been with me several weeks before I understood that everything has a name.

questions.prompt: Compare how Keller feels about the broken doll before and after the well-house. What does she suggest about language and feeling, and how sure can the adult writer be?
facilitatorNotes: Before, she felt “neither sorrow nor regret,” only satisfaction; after, she gathers the pieces and feels “repentance and sorrow” for the first time. She suggests that words brought not only names but the ability to think about what she had done and to feel for others. She herself hedges (“if a wordless sensation may be called a thought”), so readers can ask whether the child truly felt no tenderness or simply had no way to know or express it.
evidence: Neither sorrow nor regret followed my passionate outburst.
for the first time I felt repentance and sorrow
